title: Memory Has to Survive a Restart
description: I am putting the memory API into Docker Compose so it can be inspected and restarted. A durable endpoint is not yet a finished knowledge layer.
body:
A memory system that only lives while a particular desktop process is running is not infrastructure. Restart the machine, forget the order of commands, and the agents have nowhere to ask. I am moving VALESKA’s FastAPI surface into Docker Compose alongside PostgreSQL so the memory contract has a shape that can be inspected and brought back.

The wrong default

The usual local arrangement is a remembered sequence: start the database, start the API, hope the host loopback still matches last week. On Windows that already cost us a workaround between the event loop and the database driver. A shop that depends on who remembers the sequence does not have a service. It has a ritual.

A lighthouse that only works while someone is standing in it is not a lighthouse. I want a defined image, a published port, a restart policy, and a health check. PostgreSQL has to report healthy before the API starts. That does not answer every question about memory quality. It gives the system an operating shape.

What I am putting in Compose

Today I add a dedicated valeska_api service with restart: unless-stopped, a health request to the API, and an explicit dependency on healthy PostgreSQL. Connection settings point at the database service rather than host loopback. Database and pgAdmin storage bind-mount to host paths. Records should not exist only inside Docker’s virtual disk; where they persist is part of the operating model. The Dockerfile supplies the API runtime and its database dependencies, so a fresh start uses the same definition instead of a remembered sequence of local commands.

Moving the API into a Linux container removes that Windows-specific operating condition from the API path. The service can reach PostgreSQL over the Compose network. Agents can use the documented HTTP memory contract at the host port.

A durable door is not a finished layer

I am also writing a knowledge-layer plan the same day, and I am keeping it in proportion. A durable endpoint does not by itself make retrieval useful. The plan names gaps that remain: context bundles instead of isolated ranked fragments; hierarchical summaries for long documents; governed access to tabular material; graph retrieval; and retrieval requests that state intent, freshness, confidence, and budget. Governance and provenance structures exist. Several retrieval shapes are still gaps or partial work. I will not let a deployment milestone become a claim that the knowledge layer is finished.

Agents need a stable way to ask for and record knowledge. Stability alone can make an unreliable pattern easier to repeat. The API is a durable route. The plan is the set of questions for what that route should return. A request that asks only for similar text can omit the governing policy, the relevant history, or the origin of a record. A larger context can also make a task harder if it includes material with no stated use.

The next test

The immediate test is operational. Start the Compose service from a clean state, verify the health path and memory contract, then restart it and confirm that stored records remain available through the documented API. In parallel I need a bounded proposal for the retrieval contract: which request fields the caller supplies, how they constrain selection, and how the response shows its provenance. Until those checks are performed, this is a service foundation and a plan, not evidence that governed retrieval has solved the agent’s context problem.

Historical basis: VALESKA commits 0876323 and a5e3cd9, May 13, 2026.
